source.title: Estimation and Model Misspecification: Fake and Missing Features
source.authors: Martin Hellkvist; Ayça Özçelikkale; Anders Ahlén

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests double-descent behavior in linear estimation using analytical LMMSE results and experiments, rather than the deep-network methods in the original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own analytical results and experiments on estimation and held-out output MSE as model size varies. Cited double-descent findings from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study derives closed-form expected output (test) MSE for misspecified linear LMMSE/ridge estimation and runs synthetic and real-data experiments. These show a peak at n ≈ p̄ and a second descent as model size grows past it. This is a new, linear, non-deep setting with its own results on V3, V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that fake (irrelevant) features can act as regularizers and improve estimation even when the model is over-parameterized. They find that both parameter MSE and output MSE show double descent with model size. The globally optimal number of fake features for parameter MSE can be over-parameterized even though output MSE stays high regardless of the number of fake features.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses linear LMMSE estimation with random feature matrices and analyzes fake and missing features; it does not reproduce the deep-network experiments of the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior depends on the number of fake and missing features, true and assumed noise levels, and feature covariance structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Parameter-estimation MSE for the true unknowns shows double descent in the number of fake features. Its global minimum can lie deep in the over-parameterized regime even when output MSE does not improve (Figs. 4, 5, 7, 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent in parameter-estimation error can decouple from test-error double descent; the two curves can have different optima.

record.problems: The empirical liver-data experiment uses 64 rats, with 54 training and 10 held-out observations. The plotted experimental results do not report uncertainty intervals. Much of the evidence concerns a Gaussian linear-estimation setting rather than a range of model classes.
record.rows_left_out: Parameter-estimation MSE curves in Figures 4, 5, and 8 were not included because they measure error in estimated parameters rather than held-out output/test error. The study's discussion of those curves is not used as evidence for the test-error versions.

untested.parts: Deep networks: not studied at all.
Training-time (epoch) dynamics: closed-form estimators, no training curves.
No empirical sweep of sample count; evidence is analytical only.
Only linear/ridge estimators. No other model classes.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
No multiple or triple peaks. Label noise in classification is not studied; noise here is additive Gaussian or missing-feature signal.
No recounting of complexity to recover a U-shaped curve.

missing.what: Whether the peak disappears for the large-σ̂ liver curves (σ̂ = 20, 50). The text restricts double descent to small σ̂, which bears on V6 regularization removing the peak on real held-out data.

Corollary 1 and Remark 2: analytic non-monotonicity, with a local minimum at non-zero pF in the over-parameterized regime and approach to tr(Kx) from below. This is on parameter MSE; Theorem 3 and eq. (39) give the output-MSE counterpart.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this paper. Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a new linear-estimation setting, not a different method on deep networks. Figure 6 rows (r8–r10) measure parameter MSE, which is inconsistent with rows_left_out excluding parameter-MSE figures. They are kept under V6 with that caveat; for pF = 0, parameter MSE equals output MSE minus σv². No uncertainty intervals are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks and model-wise double descent in deep networks.
No empirical sweep of training sample size; the evidence is the paper's analytical output-error characterization as a function of sample count.
The study tests linear estimation, not a range of model classes.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
The study does not test multiple or triple peaks, nor whether optimally tuned regularization makes the curve disappear.
Recounting complexity by an effective parameter number to obtain an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Misspecified linear LMMSE estimator
rows.size_stated: p̄ = pS + pF; n is the number of observations
rows.operation_detail: Analytically characterize expected output MSE as sample count n varies relative to model size p̄.
rows.measure: Expected output MSE on an unseen observation
rows.value: The paper states that the output error is very large when n is close to p̄; equations (38) and (39) give expressions on either side of the threshold.
rows.note: The equations and accompanying discussion characterize the peak near n = p̄; this is analytical evidence, not an empirical sample-size sweep.
rows.check: Analytical evidence only, no sample sweep. Eq. (39) gives n/(p̄−n−1) for n < p̄, which rises with n toward the threshold, so more samples raise output MSE there. The authors say only that error is very large near n ≈ p̄; the more-data-hurts reading is inferred from the equation.

rows.note: The text describes double-descent behavior for small assumed noise levels and identifies this condition as one of the four plotted curves.
rows.check: Figure-only. The text says double descent appears for small assumed noise, but does not say which σ̂ values count as small; σ̂ = 0 and 1 are the plausible ones.

rows.subject: Misspecified linear LMMSE estimator
rows.operation_detail: Increase the number of fake features and report output MSE and its decomposition.
rows.note: The paper states that both the output MSE and the component MSEs exhibit double descent; the plotted output MSE is the held-out prediction measure.
rows.check: Output MSE falls again after the peak. However, the text says it 'stays on the same level' in the under- and over-parameterized regimes, so the second descent does not beat the first. In the caption the notation σ̂v̄* = 0 refers to the assumed noise σ̂v̄ = 0.

rows.operation_detail: Characterize analytically when the expected MSE has a peak near the interpolation threshold.
rows.value: The paper states that the peak occurs only if tr(KxC) + σv² > 0.
rows.note: The stated condition links the peak to observation noise or missing-feature signal.
rows.check: The stated condition is for parameter MSE ε (Theorem 1). Eq. (38)–(39) show the same condition governs the output-MSE peak, so the link to test error holds. The locator should add Section V.

rows.subject: Misspecified linear LMMSE estimator
rows.operation_detail: Vary the assumed noise level and report expected and empirical MSE.
rows.value: The text states that the MSEs for pF = 0 and pF = 100 are close when σ̂v̄ > 5, compared with σ̂v̄ < 5.
rows.note: The assumed noise level can damp the peak at the threshold; the paper describes this condition as a comparison with pF = 0.
rows.check: Parameter MSE, not output MSE. At the threshold (pF = 100), σ̂ > 5 brings MSE close to the pF = 0 value, so the peak is strongly damped near the optimal σ̂ ≈ 10. 'Close' is not quantified.
